passage_text: Researchers conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of the novel antihypertensive agent, Hypotensol, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. A total of 200 participants (age 35-65 years) were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive either Hypotensol 10 mg daily (n=100) or matching placebo (n=100) for 12 weeks. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups, with mean systolic blood pressure (SBP) of 145 ± 8 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) of 90 ± 6 mmHg. At week 12, the Hypotensol group exhibited a mean reduction in SBP of 12.4 mmHg (SD 5.1), whereas the placebo group showed a reduction of 3.2 mmHg (SD 4.7). The between-group difference was statistically significant (p < 0.001). Secondary outcomes included changes in heart rate and serum creatinine, both of which remained unchanged. Adverse events were mild and comparable across groups. These findings suggest that Hypotensol effectively lowers SBP in hypertensive adults without notable safety concerns.
stem: What was the mean systolic blood pressure in the Hypotensol group at week 12?
explanation: The table shows the Hypotensol group’s mean SBP at week 12 as 132.6 mmHg.
trap: Avoid confusing baseline SBP with week 12 SBP.

stem: Using the SDs of the SBP reductions and n = 100 per group, which is the approximate 95% CI (normal approximation) for the between-group difference in mean SBP reduction?
explanation: Correct: A) SE of the difference = sqrt(5.1^2/100 + 4.7^2/100) = 0.69; 9.2 +/- 1.96 x 0.69 = 7.8 to 10.6 mmHg, which excludes 0 and fits p < 0.001. Why the others are wrong: B) Uses a single-group SE (about 0.5) rather than the SE of the difference. C) Uses the SD of about 4.9 instead of the SE. D) Reports the two group means as if they were the interval.
trap: Using the SD (about 5) instead of the standard error when building the interval; that gives an interval far too wide.
